sections.section_title: Introduction to Using Geometry for Piecewise Convolution

image_slots.image_description: A clean $\tau$-axis product-overlap diagram for one fixed value of t. Show $x(\tau)$ and $h(t - \tau)$ aligned on the same horizontal $\tau$ axis, with their active overlap interval labeled from $a(t)$ to $b(t)$. Below or directly over the overlap, shade the resulting product region $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ as a simple rectangle. Label the rectangle width as $b(t)$ - $a(t)$ and the constant product height as C. Keep the diagram instructional and uncluttered; avoid decorative signal art.

blocks.text: For a direct convolution, the output at one fixed time t is found by integrating over the horizontal variable $\tau$. The value of t stays fixed while $\tau$ moves across the overlap between $x(\tau)$ and $h(t - \tau)$.

After the convolution has been split into time regions, each region has its own overlap interval. On one such region, the nonzero contribution comes only from the $\tau$-values where both factors are active.
The geometric shortcut is to look at the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$, not either signal alone. The integral is the signed area under that product over the current overlap interval.

In the simplest case, the product is constant over the whole overlap interval. Then the shaded product region is a rectangle: its width is the overlap length in $\tau$, and its height is the constant product value.

This is the recurring move for the lesson: identify the product shape for the current time region, read its geometric dimensions, compute the area, and attach that area formula to the correct piece of $y(t)$. Later sections use the same idea for rectangles, triangles, trapezoids, composite regions, and final piecewise assembly.

image_slots.image_description: A clean $\tau$-axis overlap-product diagram for the time region $0 \le t \le 1$. Show one shaded rectangular product region representing $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$. Label the horizontal $\tau$-width of the rectangle as t and the constant vertical product height as 3. Include a $\tau$ axis, the rectangle boundary, and the label $0 \le t \le 1$. Keep the visual focused on the rectangle dimensions; do not add decorative signal art or extra unused signal pieces.

example_content.example_prompt: In the shown overlap region for $0 \le t \le 1$, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a rectangle with $\tau$-width t and constant height 3. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the shaded product region is a rectangle. For this time region, the convolution contribution is the area under the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$, so use rectangle area instead of setting up a new algebraic integral.
Read the two dimensions from the product diagram: the $\tau$-width is t, and the constant product height is 3.
Multiplying the width by the height gives the value of the regional convolution integral.
So the convolution contribution on the stated region is 3t for $0 \le t \le 1$.

image_slots.image_description: A clean $\tau$-axis product-region diagram for the time region $0 \le t \le 1$. Show one shaded right-triangle region representing $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$. Label the horizontal base along the $\tau$ axis as t and label the maximum vertical product height as 2t. Include a $\tau$ axis, the triangular boundary, and the label $0 \le t \le 1$. Keep the visual focused on the triangle dimensions; do not add decorative signal art or extra unused signal pieces.

example_content.example_prompt: In the shown overlap region for $0 \le t \le 1$, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a right triangle with base t and height 2t. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the shaded product region is a triangle. The convolution contribution is still the area under the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$, but this time the product has one sloped boundary, so use triangle area instead of rectangle area.
Read the two triangle dimensions from the product diagram: the base along the $\tau$ axis is t, and the maximum product height is 2t.
Substitute the base and height from the diagram, then simplify.
So the convolution contribution on the stated region is $t^2$ for $0 \le t \le 1$.

image_slots.image_description: A clean $\tau$-axis product-region diagram for the time region $1 \le t \le 2$. Show one shaded trapezoid under the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$. Label the horizontal $\tau$-width as 1, the left vertical height as 2, and the right vertical height as t + 1. Include a $\tau$ axis, the trapezoid boundary, and the label $1 \le t \le 2$. Keep the visual focused on the trapezoid dimensions; do not add decorative signal art or extra unused signal pieces.

example_content.example_prompt: In the shown overlap region for $1 \le t \le 2$, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a trapezoid with $\tau$-width 1, left height 2, and right height t + 1. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the shaded product region is a trapezoid. The convolution contribution is still the area under $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$, but now the product has two nonzero parallel heights, so average the heights and multiply by the $\tau$-width.
Read the trapezoid dimensions from the product diagram: the $\tau$-width is 1, the left height is 2, and the right height is t + 1.
Substitute the two heights and the width, then simplify.
So the convolution contribution on the stated region is (t + 3)/2 for $1 \le t \le 2$.

sections.section_title: Splitting an Overlap Region into Geometric Pieces

image_slots.image_description: A clean $\tau$-axis product-region diagram for the time region $1 \le t \le 2$. Show one shaded composite region representing $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$, subdivided by a dashed vertical line into a rectangle plus a right triangle. Label the rectangle width as 1 and height as 2. Label the triangle base as t - 1 and height as t - 1. Include a $\tau$ axis, the decomposition line, and the label $1 \le t \le 2$. Keep the visual focused on the component dimensions; do not add decorative signal art or extra unused signal pieces.

example_content.example_prompt: In the shown overlap region for $1 \le t \le 2$, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is split into a rectangle of width 1 and height 2 plus a right triangle of base t - 1 and height t - 1. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the shaded product region is not one standard shape. Split it along the marked line, compute the area of each simple piece, and add those areas to get the convolution contribution.
Rectangle piece: the rectangle has width 1 and height 2, so its area is width times height.
Triangle piece: the right triangle has base t - 1 and height t - 1, so use one-half times base times height.
Add the component areas because the two pieces partition the same product region without overlapping interiors.
So the convolution contribution on the stated region is 2 + (1/2)(t - 1)^2, equivalently (1/2)$t^2$ - t + 5/2, for $1 \le t \le 2$.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Output from Geometric Areas

image_slots.image_description: A compact time-axis region summary for assembling a piecewise convolution output. Show the t-axis partitioned into five ordered regions: $t < 0 labeled zero overlap$, $0 \le t < 1 labeled rectangle area A_1(t)=3t$, $1 \le t < 2 labeled triangle area A_2(t)=t^2$, $2 \le t < 3 labeled trapezoid area A_3(t)=4 - t$, and $t \ge 3 labeled zero overlap$. Include a clear cue that these formulas are already computed geometric areas to be placed into $y(t)$. Keep the visual structured and symbolic; do not add decorative signal art.

example_content.example_prompt: A convolution has been split into ordered time regions. The region summary gives $A_1(t)=3t$ on $0 \le t < 1$, $A_2(t)=t^2$ on $1 \le t < 2$, and $A_3(t)=4 - t$ on $2 \le t < 3$, with zero overlap for $t < 0$ and $t \ge 3$. Assemble the complete piecewise output $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the geometric area formulas have already been computed. This step is not about finding new areas; it is about placing each area formula on its matching time interval and adding zero outside the active support.
List the regions in increasing order and keep the no-overlap regions. That gives two zero pieces and three active pieces.
Now assign each computed area formula to the interval where it was produced. The exterior regions have no overlap, so $y(t)$ is zero there.
This piecewise expression is the full LTI system output for the summarized convolution because every ordered region is covered exactly once.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a rectangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shaded product region is a rectangle, so its area is width times height. The $\tau$-width is t and the constant product height is 4.
So the convolution contribution on this region is 4t.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a rectangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shaded product region is a rectangle, so multiply its $\tau$-width by its constant product height. The $\tau$-width is 2 - t and the height is 2.
So the convolution contribution on this region is 4 - 2t.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a right triangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution contribution is the area under the product. The shaded product region is a triangle with base t and height 4t.
So the contribution from this triangular overlap region is 2t^2.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a right triangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution contribution is the area under the product. The shaded product region is a triangle with base 2 - t and height 2(2 - t).
So the contribution from this shrinking triangular overlap region is (2 - t)^2.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a trapezoid. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution contribution is the area under the product. For a trapezoid, average the two parallel heights and multiply by the $\tau$-width.
So the contribution from this trapezoidal overlap region is (t + 5)/2.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a trapezoid. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution contribution is the area under the product. Here the trapezoid has a time-dependent $\tau$-width, so keep that width in the area formula.
So the contribution from this trapezoidal overlap region is 2(3 - t).

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is split into a rectangle plus a right triangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compute each piece and add the areas because the pieces partition the same product region without overlapping interiors.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is split into a rectangle plus a right triangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compute the rectangle area and the shrinking triangle area separately, then add them.
So the convolution contribution from this composite overlap region is 3 + (1/2)(3 - t)^2.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Output from Geometric Areas

image_slots.image_description: A compact time-axis region summary for assembling a piecewise convolution output. Show the t-axis partitioned into five ordered regions: $t < -1 labeled zero overlap$, $-1 \le t < 0 labeled rectangle area A_1(t)=2(t+1)$, $0 \le t < 2 labeled constant area A_2(t)=2$, $2 \le t < 4 labeled triangle/trapezoid area A_3(t)=4 - t$, and $t \ge 4 labeled zero overlap$. Include a clear cue that these formulas are already computed geometric areas to be placed into $y(t)$. Keep the visual structured and symbolic; do not add decorative signal art.

A compact time-axis region summary for assembling a piecewise convolution output. Show the t-axis partitioned into four ordered regions: $t < 1 labeled zero overlap$, $1 \le t < 2 labeled triangular area A_1(t)=t - 1$, $2 \le t < 4 labeled shrinking area A_2(t)=(4 - t)/2$, and $t \ge 4 labeled zero overlap$. Include a clear cue that these formulas are already computed geometric areas to be placed into $y(t)$. Keep the visual structured and symbolic; do not add decorative signal art.

prompt_blocks.text: A convolution has been split into ordered time regions. The region summary gives $A_1(t)=2(t+1)$ on $-1 \le t < 0$, $A_2(t)=2$ on $0 \le t < 2$, and $A_3(t)=4 - t$ on $2 \le t < 4$, with zero overlap for $t < -1$ and $t \ge 4$. Assemble the complete piecewise output $y(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=0$ for $t < -1$; 2(t + 1) for $-1 \le t < 0$; 2 for $0 \le t < 2$; 4 - t for $2 \le t < 4$; 0 for $t \ge 4$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The area formulas are already computed. Place each formula on its matching interval, keep the intervals in increasing order, and include the two zero-overlap regions.
This covers every ordered time region exactly once.

prompt_blocks.text: A convolution has been split into ordered time regions. The region summary gives $A_1(t)=t - 1$ on $1 \le t < 2$ and $A_2(t)=(4 - t)/2$ on $2 \le t < 4$, with zero overlap for $t < 1$ and $t \ge 4$. Assemble the complete piecewise output $y(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=0$ for $t < 1$; t - 1 for $1 \le t < 2$; (4 - t)/2 for $2 \le t < 4$; 0 for $t \ge 4$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This question has two active area formulas. The assembly move is the same: assign each formula to its stated interval and add zero outside the active support.
The zero pieces are part of the complete output because there is no overlap outside the listed support.

image_records.image_description: A compact time-axis region summary for assembling a piecewise convolution output. Show the t-axis partitioned into five ordered regions: $t < 0 labeled zero overlap$, $0 \le t < 1 labeled rectangle area A_1(t)=3t$, $1 \le t < 2 labeled triangle area A_2(t)=t^2$, $2 \le t < 3 labeled trapezoid area A_3(t)=4 - t$, and $t \ge 3 labeled zero overlap$. Include a clear cue that these formulas are already computed geometric areas to be placed into $y(t)$. Keep the visual structured and symbolic; do not add decorative signal art.
image_records.report: Piecewise time-region summary for the tutorial example with three active area formulas.
image_records.lesson_core_move: Convert each time-region overlap in a direct convolution into geometric area calculations to obtain the piecewise LTI system output.
